An iOS 27 mention of a new Apple Card feature reminded me of a feature I recently had to manually turn on in a banking app, because I discovered it was disabled by default.

That feature is also related to recurring direct debit card payments, and it turns out it may not work the way we expect...

In recent years, the gradual popularisation of fintech has been one of the most practically valuable technological developments.

Once upon a time, long before banking apps existed, I had an American Express card cloned while I was in Hong Kong. A thief bought several thousand dollars' worth of jewellery, and because they were smart enough not to max out the card immediately, I had to wait over a week to receive my monthly statement before I knew anything had happened.

Luckily that one was easy to sort out: I was able to prove I had been back in England for 24 hours before the in-person transaction in Hong Kong took place, so the bank reversed the transaction straight away. But had the circumstances been different, it could have been a lot more troublesome. If the thief had maxed out the card while I was still travelling, the consequences would have been far worse.

Today, the situation is completely different. My banking app sends me a notification for every transaction, usually within 30 seconds of the purchase. Or so I thought, to be precise. As it turns out, there is one exception, and recurring transactions can slip through this notification mechanism.

If I authorise the bank to take a regular payment directly from my account, that transaction will appear in the 'recurring transactions' section of the banking app. I do check these items regularly to make sure I'm not still paying for subscriptions I no longer use.

However, if it's a recurring payment authorised on a credit card, it won't appear under the regular payment authorisations, nor will it trigger an instant notification, because the transaction isn't initiated at a payment terminal. By default, the only way to see these transactions is to manually go through your bank statements, which is not far off from the pre-fintech era.

I discovered this issue during a manual check, when I saw a credit card transaction for a subscription I had previously cancelled. For some reason, the cancellation hadn't gone through. Again, this was easy to resolve, but it did reveal a reporting loophole I'd never been aware of.

In my banking app, there turns out to be an additional transaction toggle that is disabled by default. This is completely unintuitive, because I get instant notifications for all my normal spending. Once I switched that toggle on, I started receiving notifications for recurring credit card payments.

If you want to know whether you're missing any notifications, open your banking app, go into the notification settings, and make sure all the options are turned on.
